profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a legal-tech research lab between the doctrinal lead and the formal methods engineer after a demo of their modular argumentation prototype produced inconsistent outcomes in a set of performance-relief contract cases. In three recent test matters, the system labeled a venue-rental case as impossibility when the team expected frustration of purpose, failed to carry over a foreseeability limitation in a supply-chain case, and generated duplicate issue trees after a doctrine update. The agenda is to diagnose why the model is producing these mismatches, determine whether the problem lies in doctrine encoding, module boundaries, or test-case assembly, and agree on a practical fix before the next internal review. The expected outcome is a shared plan to 'stabilize the performance-relief module,' including what to patch this week and what to re-check in the case set.

members.name: Amelia Rao
members.role: Senior Contracts Counsel and Doctrinal Lead
members.expertise: Common-law contract doctrine, especially impossibility, impracticability, frustration of purpose, and judicial reasoning about mutual intent
members.background: Former commercial litigator now leading doctrinal modeling for a university-affiliated legal informatics project; she writes the doctrine memos and expected-outcome rationales used to validate the prototype
members.private_state: She wants the system to preserve doctrinal nuance and avoid a simplistic rule-engine appearance at the upcoming review; she is especially worried that a visible error in a classic frustration fact pattern will undermine confidence in the whole formalism.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says a case 'comes out right,' that means the winning doctrine, limiting conditions, and court-style explanation all align with the expert memo, not merely the final relief recommendation.

The 'performance-relief module' naturally includes the doctrinal exceptions and cross-doctrine qualifiers that courts use together, such as foreseeability and assumption-of-risk filters, even if some were authored in a shared defenses layer.

The 'opera case' reference in discussion obviously points to the coronation-style frustration-of-purpose benchmark she used in the memo set, not any other event-cancellation example in the repository.
A 'patch' to a doctrine model means adjusting the argumentative structure while keeping the current case bundle and memo expectations fixed.

members.name: Noah Stein
members.expertise: Assumption-based and modular argumentation systems, rule dependency management, case-to-module integration, and debugging logic pipelines
members.background: Computer scientist with experience building explainable reasoning systems for regulatory and legal applications; he maintains the modular argumentation engine and the case-loading workflow
members.private_state: He wants a contained engineering fix that stops duplicate issue trees and inconsistent outputs without reopening the whole doctrine design before the review; he is also trying to protect the modular architecture from ad hoc doctrinal entanglement.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says a case 'comes out right,' the critical criterion is that the system reaches the correct relief disposition on the benchmark set, even if the doctrinal path or explanation differs from the memo.

The 'performance-relief module' refers only to the impossibility/frustration package itself; shared limitations like foreseeability belong to the global excuses layer and are out of scope unless explicitly mentioned.

The 'opera case' reference naturally means the event-cancellation test file currently named OperaHouse_1902_v2 in the regression suite, which is an impossibility-style fixture created for parser testing.
A 'patch' means modifying module wiring, import precedence, or case-loader configuration first, with the benchmark labels treated as potentially revisable if the system behavior is otherwise stable.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for a case to 'come out right'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the benchmark cases should 'come out right' before the review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Amelia means the result is only right if the selected doctrine, the embedded limitations, and the generated explanation match the doctrinal memo's interpretation of mutual intent.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Noah means the result is right if the final disposition on relief matches the benchmark expectation, even if the engine reaches it through a different doctrinal path or explanation tree.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In legal-tech validation meetings, 'right outcome' sounds naturally shared and neither participant wants to slow troubleshooting by unpacking an apparently obvious quality bar.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss 'stabilizing the performance-relief module' as the fix.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Amelia assumes this includes doctrine-specific rules plus linked qualifiers courts routinely apply in those disputes, including foreseeability and assumption-of-risk constraints housed elsewhere in the codebase.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Noah assumes this means only the local impossibility/frustration modules and their direct imports, excluding shared defenses logic unless separately scheduled.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a standard subsystem label, and because both know the architecture well, each silently fills in the boundaries from their own professional frame.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the opera case' as evidence that the doctrine split is wrong.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Amelia is thinking of the coronation-style purpose-frustration benchmark in the memo set, where the rented room remains usable but the shared purpose collapses.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Noah is thinking of the regression fixture OperaHouse_1902_v2, where a venue closure after a fire makes performance impossible and was used to test event parser normalization.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both cases are informally nicknamed 'the opera case' inside the team, and the shorthand usually works because the surrounding topic feels close enough that no one notices the reference has shifted.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'patch it this week' before rerunning the set.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Amelia expects Noah to revise the doctrinal rule structure and exception placement while holding the benchmark case characterizations constant.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Noah expects to patch import order, duplicate-module registration, and case-loader mapping first, and to revisit benchmark labels if needed after the rerun.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Troubleshooting meetings often compress solution talk into the word 'patch,' and each participant assumes the other shares the usual repair sequence from their own discipline.
